articles.text: Editor: For generations, Piedmont’s local government has operated on a simple premise: the City Council is a non-partisan, volunteer-driven body dedicated to the stewardship of our small and unique community. Council members are not chosen based on party affiliations, partisan platforms, or external political endorsements. Council members are our neighbors and friends — citizens who volunteer endless hours overseeing Piedmont’s infrastructure, managing the budget, adopting city policies, and ensuring public safety. However, I have noticed a concerning shift in this year’s Piedmont City Council race — partisan politics creeping into what has historically been a local, non-partisan space. For instance, the endorsement of Piedmont City Council candidate Adam Hundt by the Alameda County Democratic Party, alongside various current and former regional Democratic officeholders. While candidate endorsements are standard practice in county, state, and federal elections, introducing formal political parties into a Piedmont City Council race could fundamentally change the dynamics of how our town governs itself. When political party apparatuses enter local non-partisan elections, several concerns arise: • Outside Influence: By seeking or accepting the backing of a regional political party, this invites outside political interests into Piedmont where decisions should be made exclusively by and for Piedmont residents. • Erosion of Independent Governance: An effective, non-partisan Council fosters independent thinking and constructive problem-solving among fellow residents. When members lean on political party affiliations and/or political networks outside of Piedmont, it risks introducing ideological divides and conflicts into Piedmont’s civic life. Piedmont is a special community. Our civic strength lies in our ability to sit across the table from one another as neighbors and friends — not as Democrats, Republicans, or Independents - and address local challenges with common sense, independent thinking and civic pride. To preserve what makes Piedmont special, we must maintain the integrity of our local non-partisan traditions. Our Council members should be accountable solely to the residents of Piedmont — free from the influence of outside political party affiliations. As Piedmont voters mark this year’s election ballot, it is worth asking whether we stand for preserving a non-partisan City Council driven purely by local volunteerism — or allowing outside political party politics to dictate our local governance.
articles.title: Preserving Piedmont’s non-partisan tradition

articles.text: Dear Editor: Safe streets, dependable emergency services, and well-maintained public spaces take investment. That’s why we’re voting yes on Measure GG. Mayor Betsy Andersen recently shared a number that puts the challenge in perspective: of every dollar we pay in base property taxes, just 18 cents comes back to the City of Piedmont. Piedmont also brings in less revenue per resident than Oakland, Berkeley, or Emeryville. With no significant commercial or retail tax base, we have limited ways to fund our police, firefighters, parks, streets, and aging infrastructure. Measure GG, unanimously endorsed by our mayor, all members of the City Council, and ten former Mayors, would raise the one-time real estate transfer tax from 1.3% to 1.75%, bringing it closer to rates in surrounding communities. Paid when real property is sold, the tax can be split between buyer and seller. The increase would generate an estimated $1.5 million annually for essential city services and maintenance. We believe this is a practical investment in the community we love and call home. Please join us in voting yes on Measure GG. –Dan and Jill Saper

articles.text: Editor: What kind of person do I want to be on the City Council? I want someone who has experience working in a variety of different work environments. A person who has worked as a novice through managerial and leadership positions. A person who demonstrates competence and expertise in their field and also in allied fields of their profession. A person who has not only an interest in their own work but also an interest in the work of those with whom they work. I want someone who understands that he represents each and every one of his city neighbors. Even within our small city, we have divergent neighborhood needs and wants. All of these require the same effort and diligence. I want someone who is an excellent and transparent communicator. A person who says what he means and does what he says. A person who is a good listener, who pays attention to the requests of his neighbors, and understands the importance of solving problems as they see them. I want a person who understands the complexity of city governance, the many different areas and variables that must work together as a whole to satisfy the needs of all. articles.text: Join Pardee Home Museum for a look at a historical map developed by Liam O’Donoghue, East Bay Yesterday podcaster of Long Lost Oakland. articles.text: Councilmember Tom Ramsey is running for re-election to the City Council in this November’s General Election. Ramsey has lived in Piedmont for over 30 years and, alongside his architectural work, has volunteered for the City of Piedmont for 11 years on the Planning Commission and City Council. He’s committed to finishing the work he started in his first term. Ramsey grew up in the Rust Belt in northeastern Ohio, where his family had a legacy of tire making. Ramsey was the generation that left the tire-making business, deciding to attend college in Ohio at the University of Cincinnati. He graduated from the university with a degree in architecture in 1987. A few years later, Ramsey got married and moved to the Bay Area, landing in Piedmont in 1993, where he raised his two daughters. Ramsey worked for an architecture firm in San Francisco before partnering with a few colleagues to start his own architectural firm, RPR Architects. He spent 18 years at the firm working with tech companies and local governments, helping plan and build their commercial projects. Ramsey left the firm in 2013 to join Project Management Advisors, Inc., a real estate and project management firm that specializes in helping companies manage their projects. Ramsey remains with the company as the acting Vice President and Managing Director. “I help a lot of tech companies build pretty cool stuff in the Bay Area,” said Ramsey. As his daughters attended Piedmont’s schools, Ramsey worked on PUSD’s Seismic Safety program, which strengthened or replaced school facilities to meet safety standards. According to Ramsey, the Planning Director at the time approached him after his work on the project and asked him to apply for the Planning Commission. “I didn’t get on the first or second time. The third time I applied, they accepted me. It was pretty competitive,” said Ramsey. Ramsey volunteered for seven years on the Planning Commission and served one term as the chair in 2018. Under his tenure, he updated the land use design guidelines that, according to Ramsey, hadn’t been updated in roughly 40 years. “It was a lot of work. We had a consulting architect, a consulting planner, and completely redid them. I thought it was a good foundation for when I joined the council,” said Ramsey. Ramsey was elected to the City Council in November 2022 and spent his first few years learning the job and understanding what it takes to be a successful governing body. “It’s really important to be able to work together with everybody on council,” Ramsey continued. “It’s important to hire the right department heads because I think in a small town those positions are really accessible to the public too, which I think is really an advantage. We have great people not only doing the work but Tom Ramsey working with the community as well.” Ramsey took his time deciding whether he wanted to run for re-election, not wanting to commit to something he wasn’t fully invested in. Ultimately, he decided to try for a second term because he wants to finish what he started on the council, citing the Moraga Canyon specific plan as a project he’d like to continue overseeing. “I didn’t make that decision until I knew I was 100% in, and I am. I know the amount of work that’s involved, so I wanted to be sure that I was prepared to do that,” said Ramsey. Outside of his architectural work and City Council commitments, Ramsey enjoys riding his e-bike and hiking the trails of Redwood and Tilden parks. articles.text: The Post spoke with former Piedmont Mayor and budget advisory committee member Bob McBain about the misinformation surrounding Measure GG. The proposed measure would increase Piedmont’s transfer tax from 1.3% ($13 per $1,000) to 1.75%, generating $1.5 million for the city’s general fund. The transfer tax is only paid when a home is sold. McBain addressed the false claim that the measure would drive up home prices in Piedmont. “What drives up home prices is supply and demand,” he said. “In Piedmont, housing supply is limited, and demand for housing is high, resulting in high prices for real estate.” Piedmont’s demand is high because “Piedmont is a desirable place to live. The facilities (parks, playfields, community spaces) and high level of services (police, fire, public works) available to our residents are the reason Piedmont is desirable. These facilities and services are paid for, in part, by the current transfer tax. The proposed increase to the transfer tax is modest and would align Piedmont’s transfer tax with the rate currently charged in Oakland for properties with sales prices between $2-5 million.” He added, “The City of Piedmont currently has a transfer tax of 1.3% per $1,000 that was set 33 years ago. The difference from the current rate to the new rate for a $2.5 million home sale in Piedmont would be $11,250.” McBain rejected the false claim that purchasing a home upfront would increase by some fixed arbitrary number. “That is a completely made-up cost. I have no idea where that number is coming from,” said McBain. McBain concluded by stating, “Proceeds from Measure GG will stay in Piedmont and support our core City services through the City’s General Fund. The city uses transfer tax revenues to partially pay for repair of aging city buildings, streets and sidewalks, parks, public safety, and recreation.” Readers can read the exact details on Measure GG on the city’s website.
articles.title: Former Piedmont Mayor addresses false claims on Measure GG

The event will take place at the Zion Lutheran Church, 5201 Park Blvd. in Piedmont. The free community event will include indoor and outdoor activities, with opportunities to view stars, clusters, nebulae, and galaxies through telescopes provided by the East Bay Astronomical Society. No previous astronomy experience is necessary. Participants are also welcome to bring their own telescope or binoculars. In addition to stargazing, guests can create their own star charts and planet maps and participate in a variety of astronomy-themed activities. Hot chocolate, constellation cookies, and other snacks will be available throughout the evening. “Whether you are an experienced sky watcher or have never looked through a telescope before, the Star Party is a chance to slow down, look up, and discover the wonders of the night sky,” said Steve Harger, Director of Family Ministries at Zion Lutheran Church. For more information, contact Zion Lutheran Church at 510- 530-4213 or visit zionlutheran. net. The proposed measure would increase Piedmont’s transfer tax from 1.3% ($13 per $1,000) to 1.75%, generating $1.5 million for the city’s general fund. The transfer tax is only paid when a home is sold. McBain addressed the false claim that the measure would drive up home prices in Piedmont. “What drives up home prices is supply and demand,” he said. “In Piedmont, housing supply is limited, and demand for housing is high, resulting in high prices for real estate.” Piedmont’s demand is high because “Piedmont is a desirable place to live. The facilities (parks, playfields, community spaces) and high level of services (police, fire, public works) available to our residents are the reason Piedmont is desirable. These facilities and services are paid for, in part, by the current transfer tax. The proposed increase to the transfer tax is modest and would align Piedmont’s transfer tax with the rate currently charged in Oakland for properties with sales prices between $2-5 million.” He added, “The City of Piedmont currently has a transfer tax of 1.3% per $1,000 that was set 33 years ago. The difference from the current rate to the new rate for a $2.5 million home sale in Piedmont would be $11,250.” McBain rejected the false claim that purchasing a home upfront would increase by some fixed arbitrary number. “That is a completely made-up cost. I have no idea where that number is coming from,” said McBain. McBain concluded by stating, “Proceeds from Measure GG will stay in Piedmont and support our core City services through the City’s General Fund. The city uses transfer tax revenues to partially pay for repair of aging city buildings, streets and sidewalks, parks, public safety, and recreation.” Readers can read the exact details on Measure GG on the city’s website. articles.text: Wins Boys 12-13 age group, earns trip to Augusta National Piedmont student Jamison Takazawa won 1st place in the 12-13 age group during the September 20 Regional Qualifier of the Drive, Chip, and Putt competition at Pebble Beach. He has earned a trip to Augusta, Georgia, to compete in the national final prior to the Masters Golf Tournament. Takazawa finished tied for first with Malcolm Russell of Shelby, Montana during the Regional Qualifier and had to earn his trip to Augusta National by sinking a 15-foot putt in a tiebreaker. Takazawa said he officially started playing golf at age five, but his love for the game started before that. “When I was little, I insisted on bringing my plastic golf clubs to preschool every day. I guess I just couldn’t leave them behind,” said Takazawa. During the pandemic daily trips to the golf range with his dad helped things to click for Takazawa. For the Piedmont fifth grader, just getting to the Pebble Beach Regional Qualifier was a test in its own. Takazawa told the Post the qualifying started with 33 local qualifying events, each with 30-40 kids competing. The top three golfers from each local qualifier advanced to one of seven subregional competitions, and only the top two from each subregional made it to Pebble Beach. “When you do the math, roughly 1,000 to 1,300 kids started the journey, and I was lucky enough to be one of the final 14 at Pebble Beach! Then, to actually win at Pebble Beach and earn a spot in the National Finals at Augusta National? That’s something I still can’t believe! Pebble Beach was already a dream come true, but knowing I’ll get to compete at Augusta, where I’ve watched my golf heroes play, makes it even more special,” he said. Takazawa showed his mental toughness and positive attitude, especially during the driving aspect of the competition. “Right when my group competed, the wind came howling! It was crazy! But the funny thing is, I actually love playing in crazy winds. I practice at Metro and Takazawa’s had the same putt in the tiebreaker as he had missed earlier in the competition. “I already knew the break and exactly where I needed to aim. The tricky part was hitting the ball hard enough to keep it above the hole and hold my line. That’s a scary putt because if you miss, the ball could roll way past the hole. But I knew I couldn’t play scared,” he said. Takazawa nailed the putt and punched his ticket to compete at the most storied course in the country, if not the world, Augusta National, home of the Masters. Bobby Jones, 1920’s amateur golfer, famously said, “Competitive golf is played mainly on a five-and-a-half-inch course... the space between your ears.” Takazawa, still in 5th grade, has a mental edge on the course that will serve him in all walks of life. He competed in the 12-13 group at Pebble Beach, at the age of 11, because he will be 12 during the finals in April. “You can’t always control what happens to you, but you can control how you respond. The biggest lesson golf has taught me is that even when you’re in a bad spot, you can still make something great happen. Sometimes you just have to change how you look at it!” he said. Takazawa is one of 80 junior golfers (7-15 years old) set to compete in the 13th annual Drive, Chip and Putt National Finals at Augusta on April 4, 2027, the Sunday before the Masters Tournament. He is one of 10 finalist in the boys 12-13 age group, national champions in each group will be decided after participants hit three drives, three chips, and three putts. Photos by Drive, Chip and Putt Jamison Takazawa celebrates after sinking a putt during the Drive, Chip and Putt regional qualifier at Pebble Beach. Monarch Golf Courses, where wind is pretty much part of the experience. So when the wind picked up, I remember thinking, ‘Hey, I’ve played in this before!’ I played a lower fairway-finder drive that the wind didn’t affect as much, and I got all 3 drives to score,” he said. When Takazawa found out he was tied for first with 138 points and was heading into a playoff for the one spot at Augusta National he rose to the challenge. “I knew this was my moment. It was basically ‘do or die.’ One putt could decide whether I’d go to Augusta! But the funny thing is, I wasn’t scared at all. I was excited for the challenge,” he said. articles.text: Staff Photos Mateo Long finished with two touchdowns on six receptions for 123 yards against Tennyson. Cyrus Emanuelson passed for 205 yards and four touchdowns. The Highlanders’ football team fell short of a comeback win by two points in a 35-33 loss to Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division foes Tennyson, at the Lancers’ field in Hayward on Friday, October 23. It marks Piedmont’s second consecutive loss, coming narrowly within beating the division leaders. Despite the loss, it was a solid response to their 20-3 loss at Castro Valley the previous week. Now with a 2-6 overall record and 1-2 record against Mission Division teams, PHS must beat Alameda in the season-finale on November 6 to secure a chance at gaining a North Coast Section bid. Before that, PHS visits Pinole Valley in Pinole, which is on a three-game winning streak at 3-5 overall. Against the Lancers, if one or two plays went Piedmont’s way, the result could’ve easily swung in the other direction. The Highlanders notably scored 19 points in the fourth quarter. It was a huge game for receiver Mateo Long, scoring two touchdowns on six receptions for 123 yards. Game Recap Piedmont trailed 14-7 through the first quarter and 21-14 by halftime time. The Lancers extended the lead to 29-14 in the third quarter, while PHS added 19 points in the final going but conceded six. Tennyson recovered an onside kick to start the game and scored in nine plays, making it 6-0 after a failed two-point conversion. PHS responded with an eightplay, 72-yard drive that featured converting a 3rd-and-14 with a 14-yard pass from Cyrus Emanuelson to Max Fujimoto. They scored on a 3rd-and-12 from their own 49, where Long caught a slant route over the middle to sprint 51 yards to the house – giving PHS a 7-6 lead. Henry Brennan intercepted a Tennyson pass on the Lancers’ third play of its next possession, but Tennyson grabbed an interception of its own on Piedmont’s ensuing series and returned it to the six-yard line. That enabled a THS touchdown on its first play, making it 14-7 after a two-point conversion. The Highlanders committed another turnover with a fumble at the Lancers’ 33 on their next possession. However, Piedmont’s George Saunders punched out a fumble on a long Tennyson run, leading to a recovery to their own 24. After trades of possession, the Lancers scored to make it 21-7 midway through the second. PHS answered with an exhaustive 16-play series for 64 yards, scoring on a three-yard pass to Diego Hurwitz – making it 21-14. PHS recovered an onside kick to start the third quarter, but turned over on downs at the Lancers’ 28. The series had a critical missed connection between Emanuelson and Fujimoto, where the receiver had an open lane to the end zone, but the throw was low and dropped. Tennyson scored in seven plays to take a 29-14 lead after George Saunders had a touchdown reception and a forced fumble. a two-point conversion. It led to PHS scoring on an 11-play, 72 yard series that included a 24-yard reception by Saunders on 3rd-and-5, while Colby Hong finished with a one-yard touchdown carry early in the fourth quarter – making it 29-20 after a missed point after attempt. Piedmont forced a punt on the Lancers’ next possession, leading to a 69-yard touchdown drive on eight plays. PHS converted a 4th-and-1 at their own 40 on a three-yard reception by Rehan Mumtaz, and a 3rd-and-14 on a pass to Long. They scored on a 30-yard reception by Long, similarly on a slant over the middle and breaking three tackles on his way to the end zone. A fumbled point after attempt cut the deficit to 29-26. However, Tennyson scored on its second play of the next drive, this time on a huge 85-yard sweep down the right side to make it 35-26. Piedmont scored near the final minute with a 50 yard series on six plays. It capped off with Saunders grabbing a pass on a jump-ball at its peak for a fiveyard touchdown. Tennyson recovered the ensuing onside kick, and killed the clock. Final stats: Emanuelson completed 15 of 24 passes for 205 yards and four touchdowns. Vaha Mafi had 13 carries for 79 yards. Mumtaz had 38 rushing yards and two receptions for nine yards. Hong scored one rushing touchdown. Hurwitz had two receptions for eight yards and a touchdown. Saunders had two receptions for 31 yards, one touchdown, and a forced fumble. Fujimoto had two receptions for 21 yards. Long had six receptions for 123 yards and two touchdowns. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-6 overall, 1-2 league) visits Pinole Valley in Pinole on Friday, October 30 at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Highlanders get No. 3 seed in North Coast Section playoffs Piedmont High’s volleyball team closed its regular season in a big way, defeating Alameda 3-1 at Binks Rawlings Gym on Thursday, October 22. The win avenges a 3-0 loss to the Hornets earlier this month on October 6. “The team knew they had a shot. They didn’t play well at Alameda. It came together pretty well, everyone played clean and consistent. It was for sure the program’s best win of the year,” said co-head coach Mike Glass. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 15-13 overall to close its season, moving them into the Division 3 North Coast Section postseason as the No. 3 seed. They opened their postseason campaign last night against San Leandro on the road. The Pirates gained the right to host by winning the Western Alameda County Conference’s Shoreline Division. Results were not complete by Post time, but will be covered in next week’s Post. The Highlanders beat the Pirates 3-1 on September 8, but San Leandro notably went perfect 8-0 against Shoreline teams. Piedmont resides in the WACC’s Foothill Division, reserved for the conference’s best teams. “We’re expecting a competitive match. We beat them, but we were at home, and it’s much easier to play at home. San Leandro is a very good team with two solid outside hitters. They could’ve easily beat us, so we just have to stay focused,” Glass said. Against Alameda, the Highlanders were without starting middle Charlotte Bailey. Stepping into her spot was Izara Dando, recording eight kills on the night. It was also a big match for sophomore Emilia Angulo, who was called up from the Junior Varsity team in recent weeks. She finished second on the team in kills against Alameda with nine. “We had to play without our starting middle, but the team adjusted really well. Izara stepped in and did a fantastic job. Emi is a call-up JV player and is a consistent offensive player. She’s athletic, tall, and has great reach and consistency,” Glass said. Match Recap Piedmont won by scores of 25-23, 19-25, 25-22, 25-19. In the first set, Alameda controlled much of the set and held a 16-11 lead before Piedmont turned things around. From there, PHS scored six straight points to go up 17-16 that featured to aces by Olivia Stevens and a kill by Lucia Dorsey. Alameda tied at 22-22, but Piedmont closed with three of the final four points, featuring a kill by Angulo. PHS led much of the second set, but alameda took the lead at 17-16 and scored the final eight of 11 points. Henry Brennan intercepted a Tennyson pass on the Lancers’ third play of its next possession, but Tennyson grabbed an interception of its own on Piedmont’s ensuing series and returned it to the six-yard line. The series had a critical missed connection between Emanuelson and Fujimoto, where the receiver had an open lane to the end zone, but the throw was low and dropped. Tennyson scored in seven plays to take a 29-14 lead after George Saunders had a touchdown reception and a forced fumble. a two-point conversion. Piedmont forced a punt on the Lancers’ next possession, leading to a 69-yard touchdown drive on eight plays. PHS converted a 4th-and-1 at their own 40 on a three-yard reception by Rehan Mumtaz, and a 3rd-and-14 on a pass to Long. They scored on a 30-yard reception by Long, similarly on a slant over the middle and breaking three tackles on his way to the end zone. A fumbled point after attempt cut the deficit to 29-26. Saunders had two receptions for 31 yards, one touchdown, and a forced fumble. Fujimoto had two receptions for 21 yards. Long had six receptions for 123 yards and two touchdowns. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team wrapped up a busy week with a pair of events. They competed at 2026 Mid-Season Mania Invitational at Campolindo in Moraga on Wednesday, October 21 and the Haystack Tune-Up at Hayward High on Saturday, October 24. The Mid-Season Mania was a 3200 meter event on Campolindo’s track, while the Haystack Tune-Up is a precursor to the Western Alameda County Conference Championship on November 7. The event is run on the same Hayward High course as the championship race. “We had some outstanding performances across the team, including numerous personal records and some terrific individual efforts,“ said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “With our championship meets approaching, it was especially exciting to see so many runners competing well, racing with determination, and continuing to improve. The Hayward course will also host our WACC and NCS Championships, making Saturday’s performances particularly encouraging as we head into the final weeks of the season.” Haystack Tune-Up results The boys’ team finished 15th of 21 schools at the event. The girls’ only brought three runners, making them ineligible to score as a team, but still did well on an individual basis. On the boys’ side, sophomore Dylan Wallway led the group in 52nd of 178 runners with a time of 16:56.4 on the three-mile course. “Dylan Wallway deserves special recognition for an outstanding race, emerging as our top boys’ performer this weekend. Dylan dug deep, gave everything he had, and delivered a determined, gutsy performance. There was nothing easy about his effort, and it demonstrated just how much he’s willing to push himself to compete at a high level,” Zirkelbach said. Behind Wallway was junior Aaron Bennett finishing 58th in 17:07.3. It marked Bennett’s first event since the season-opening meet on September 5 after dealing with an illness. “It was great to see Aaron Bennett back racing after several weeks of illness. articles.text: Piedmont‘s boys’ water polo team ended its regular season with an 8-6 win over rival Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 20 at the Piedmont Pool. The result brings the Highlanders’ record to 11-10 overall and 4-2 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. They moved into the WACC Tournament with the No. 3 seed and faced Castro Valley in the opening round yesterday, October 27, at the San Leandro pool. Results were not complete by Post time, but will be covered in next week’s Post. With a win on Tuesday, Piedmont will face the winner of No. 2 Berkeley and No. 7 Lick-Wilmerding. The Highlanders faced the Yellowjackets twice during the regular season, losing both games by just one goal, a 10-9 defeat on September 4 and a 13-12 loss on September 29. “We’ve been preaching defensive principles, like getting into our lanes and getting our hands up. We want them to be ballhawks, and they’ve really taken to that,” coach Rik Krumins said. Match Recap Piedmont started off hot with the first four goals of the game, leading 3-0 by the end of the first quarter and 6-2 by halftime. The Dragons clawed back to cut the deficit to 7-4 to start the fourth quarter, while Piedmont scored once in the final going and allowed two goals. It was a defensive battle through much of the first quarter with Piedmont finally breaking the deadlock with 2:36 remaining when Henry Stein launched in a shot. PHS quickly added another slightly over a minute later with Rylan Patty scoring, while Stein scored his second with 48 seconds left. Stein made it 4-0 nearly two minutes into the second quarter at the 5:08 mark. Bishop O’Dowd landed a pair of goals to cut Piedmont’s lead to 4-2 with 3:19 before halftime, but Piedmont scored the final two goals of the quarter by Henry Van Den Bos at 1:25 and Patty with 53 seconds left. In the third quarter, O’Dowd scored after one minute and logged another goal with 4:26 remaining to cut Piedmont’s lead to 6-4. Van Den Bos helped PHS keep a three-goal advantage, scoring with 31 seconds left. O’Dowd scored again with 4:08 left in the fourth quarter, and then put itself one-goal behind with 2:39 left in the game, 7-6. After back and forth possessions in the final two minutes of the game, Patty helped solidify the win with 57 seconds left. Final scorers: Stein and Patty both finished with three goals, while Van Den Bos had two. articles.text: Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing, the most comprehensive retrospective to date of the artist’s body of work, is on view now at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA). The exhibition features half a century of work by Hassinger, including large-scale sculpture, site-specific installation, video, and performance, and will display more than twenty of her most notable works from the 1970s to the present. Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing will be accompanied by an extensive exhibition catalogue, featuring new scholarly essays and previously unpublished documentation of her artwork. Notable displayed works include Love (2008), a site-specific sculpture composed of pink plastic bags inflated by human breath and filled with love notes; Beach (1980), a floor installation consisting of plaster and wooden dowels; and multiple sculptures that incorporate recently harvested tree branches which BAMPFA showcases in partnership with the University of California Botanical Garden. “Maren Hassinger’s practice has been of great influence for generations of artists,” Chief Curator Margot Norton said in a press release. “We are thrilled to finally bring her artworks and their stories from across her career together through our exhibition, and to showcase Hassinger’s profound contributions to contemporary art.” “Maren Hassinger’s work invites us to reflect on the beauty and complexity of human connection, through movement, material, and shared experience,” said BAMPFA’s Executive Director, Julie Rodrigues Widholm. “Presenting this landmark retrospective at BAMPFA underscores our commitment to amplifying artists whose practices challenge conventions and inspire collective engagement across generations.” The retrospective is on display at BAMPFA now through November 29. More information about this and other public programs can be found at bampfa.org. Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing installation view at BAMPFA. articles.text: The Treasure Island Museum will host a happy hour fundraiser featuring live jazz, craft cocktails and tours of historic Building One on Friday, November 13, from 5 to 7 p.m. at 39 Treasure Island Road in San Francisco. The event will include a no-host bar serving alcoholic and nonalcoholic drinks and snacks in Gold Bar Whiskey’s tasting room. Museum Director John Hogan will lead a free tour of Building One at 5:30 p.m., followed by a tour of the museum’s current exhibition at 6:30 p.m. The exhibition features works by artists who appeared on Treasure Island during the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition. An optional cocktail-making class featuring Gold Bar Whiskey will begin at 3:45 p.m. and requires a separate ticket. Building One, completed in 1938, originally served as the administrative center for the Golden Gate International Exposition, a world’s fair celebrating the Pacific region. It later served as a terminal for Pan American Airways and as headquarters for the U.S. Navy’s Twelfth Naval District. The Art Moderne-style building is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The nonprofit Treasure Island Museum preserves the island’s history through exhibits, tours, educational programs and online resources. Its collection covers the world’s fair, the island’s aviation history and its decades as a naval installation. The museum is also working toward developing a larger permanent museum space in Building One. Proceeds from the fundraiser will support the museum’s programs and ongoing efforts to preserve and share Treasure Island’s history. Registration for the happy hour is available at https://www. treasureislandmuseum.org/. Courtesy of Treasure Island Museum The event will include a no-host bar serving alcoholic and nonalcoholic drinks.

articles.text: Visitors to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) can make their own kites with artist Jacob Hashimoto during a free workshop November 7, held inside his large-scale installation Giant Arc. The workshop runs from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. in the museum’s Roberts Family Gallery. Hashimoto will lead the kite-making activity from 11 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., with additional time afterward for participants to continue creating. No prior experience is required, and the event is open to all ages. Museum admission is not required. The workshop takes place inside Jacob Hashimoto: Giant Arc, the largest installation of the artist’s career. The work comprises more than 70,000 handmade kites constructed from bamboo and specialized paper, suspended together in a floating canopy that fills the gallery from floor to ceiling and wall to wall. The kites feature a range of shapes, including squares, cirJacob Hashimoto cles and hexagons, with patterns inspired by the Bay Area landscape. The installation invites visitors to experience the interplay of color, pattern and movement as they walk beneath the suspended forms. “This giant arc of kites, color and pattern will be at once chaotic and meditative, playful and considered — a generous artwork that invites viewers to spend time Photo by Don Ross in the gallery,” Hashimoto said of the installation when it was unveiled in August. The museum commissioned the work for its ground-floor Roberts Family Gallery, a free public space designed to welcome visitors of all ages. For more information about the Nov. 7 workshop, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/event/make-akite-with-jacob-hashimoto/.

articles.text: Performances take place at the Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts in Oakland. Cal Performances will present the West Coast premiere of South African artist William Kentridge’s theater production The Head & the Load November 12 through 15 at the Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts in Oakland. The multidisciplinary work examines the history of more than 2 million Africans who fought and died during World War I. The production combines dance, projections, speech, song, shadow play, costumes and music to explore the effects of colonialism and war. Directed and conceived by Kentridge, the production features choreography by Gregory Maqoma and music composed by Philip Miller and Thuthuka Sibisi. Its score combines traditional African songs, European compositions, war chants and percussion. The libretto draws on texts from anticolonial writers, Dada poets and Setswana proverbs. The production takes its title from a Ghanaian proverb: “The head and the load are the troubles of the neck.” Kentridge has described the work as an effort to document the experiences of Black participants whose contributions to the war have often been overlooked. The Head & the Load premiered in 2018 at Tate Modern in London, followed by performances at New York City’s Park Avenue Armory that year. The Oakland performances mark its West Coast premiere. A 180-foot stage will be constructed in the Kaiser Center’s arena to accommodate the production. The performances also launch a five-season Cal Performances initiative to present a different interdisciplinary work by Kentridge each season. The organization previously presented his Sibyl in 2023 and The Great Yes, The Great No in 2025. Kentridge will participate in a free pre-performance conversation with Debarati Sanyal, director of UC Berkeley’s Center for Interdisciplinary Critical Inquiry, from 6 to 7 p.m. November 13. The discussion will address the production’s historical context and its relationship to the season’s Illuminations theme. The event is free to ticket holders for that evening’s performance. Performances are scheduled for 7:30 p.m. November 12-14 and 3 p.m. November 15 at the Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts, 10 10th St., Oakland. Tickets are available at calperformances.org or by calling the box office at 510-642-9988. articles.text: Tour includes SF dates in November with SF Symphony Alonzo King LINES Ballet will join the San Francisco Symphony for three performances in November featuring two world premieres choreographed by Alonzo King, the San Francisco-based dance company’s founder and artistic director. The performances are scheduled for Nov. 19-21 at Davies Symphony Hall, where the company will present new works set to Claude Debussy’s Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune and Aaron Copland’s suite from Appalachian Spring. James Gaffigan will conduct the Symphony. The program also includes Sergei Prokofiev’s Sinfonia concertante, featuring San Francisco Symphony Principal Cellist Rainer Eudeikis. The November performances are part of LINES Ballet’s 2026- 27 national tour and continue the company’s longstanding collaboration with the Symphony. The organizations have collaborated five times since 2020, including three mainstage performances. “Returning to collaborate with the San Francisco Symphony feels both like a homecoming and an evolution of a shared artistic language,” King said in a press release. He described the new works as an opportunity to explore how movement and sound interact through live performance. LINES Ballet’s broader national tour features four works by King: LEGACY, a collaboration with jazz bassist, vocalist and composer esperanza spalding; Ode to Alice Coltrane, a tribute to the composer, pianist and spiritual leader; Ma Mère l’Oye (Mother Goose), set to Maurice Ravel’s score; and Deep River, created with Grammy Award-winning vocalist Lisa Fischer and jazz pianist and composer Jason Moran. The San Francisco Symphony performances will take place at 7:30 p.m. each evening at Davies Symphony Hall. Visit www.linesballet.org to purchase tickets. The tour will showcase four signature works from Alonzo King’s repertoire. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) opens its 90th Anniversary Season on Saturday, November 7, 2026, at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. articles.text: The dreary overcast sky and cool fall weather on October 21 did not dampen the spirits of the intrepid Walking on Wednesday group, thanks to the walk’s leader, 33-year-old Max Becker. His bright smile and musical talent brightened everyone’s spirits. A founding member of his Piedmont family’s internationally renowned punk rock band, SWMRS, Max brought along his acoustic guitar and the lyrics to four popular tunes. Soon he had the walkers belting out the opening lines of My Girl by The Temptations (1964): “I’ve got sunshine on a cloudy day, when it’s cold outside I’ve got the month of May.” Lois Price led us in specially choreographed movements to the song. Everyone had a good time singing and grooving to the beat, and we probably entertained anybody passing by the Exedra as well. After warming up our vocal cords and our bodies, the walkers headed north on Highland Avenue towards Moraga Avenue, made a right onto Moraga, and stopped at the corner of Monte Avenue and Moraga. We wanted to view the huge bald eagles’ nest in the tallest eucalyptus tree on the boundary between Mountain View Cemetery and Piedmont. In 2025 an eagle pair successfully hatched and raised two chicks in the nest, but in 2026 the couple’s eggs did not hatch despite diligent care by the parents. A neighbor reported that he spotted both adult birds separately in the nest about a week ago, and a local bird expert said he saw them together in the nest on October 18—a very good sign, since bald eagle courtship and nest building in California usually happen from October through December, with egg laying typically occurring from January to February. To encourage the bald eagle couple, Max led the Wednesday Walkers in Take It Easy by the Eagles (1972). As cars drove by on Moraga Avenue and home construction noise rang out, we sang, “Take it easy, take it easy. Don’t let the sound of your own wheels drive you crazy.” The walkers posed for our group photo and headed south on Monte towards Park Way, sending positive thoughts to the birds for a successful breeding season in 2027. We also enjoyed all the Halloween decorations at the festive houses along the way, spotting lots of ghosts and spiders, as well as a two-inch-long real-life spider in a web in an oak thicket on Moraga. We turned left at Park Way and trudged up to Pala Avenue where we climbed several flights of stairs to upper Scenic Avenue. We made a left on Scenic, and many walkers stopped to admire the gorgeous 270-degree view of San Francisco Bay at the spot where Scenic makes a sharp turn to the right. The walkers could see Alameda and Oakland to the south, then west across the Bay Bridge to San Francisco, north across the Golden Gate Bridge to Mt. Tamalpais in Marin County, and then east across the Richmond–San Rafael Bridge back to the East Bay. The group continued up Scenic to where it meets Alta at a circular intersection we nicknamed “The Top of the World.” This was the stage Max Max Becker and Lois Price grooving at the Exedra. Bill Ahern loves the “Elderly at Play” sign on Scenic Avenue. Group photo at Moraga and Monte Avenues near bald eagles’ nest. articles.text: What if participating in the arts could be good not only for our spirits, but also for our health and even our healthcare budgets? An approach called social prescribing connects people with community activities, including music, theater and art classes, to support their well-being. Massachusetts has helped pioneer the approach through programs such as CultureRx. Research highlighted by the Massachusetts Cultural Council estimates that every dollar invested in arts-on-prescription programs can generate $2.30 to $4.43 in economic benefits. Other reported findings include a 56% decrease in anxiety and depression and a 74% reduction in loneliness among participants. With the creative arts playing an essential role in community health, what steps must we take to secure their future? Alongside making them accessible to all communities, how do we ensure they remain available to everyone in the years ahead? For Stagebridge, the Oakland performing arts nonprofit approaching its 50th anniversary, that question is central to planning for the future. That’s why Stagebridge recently brought together local and national arts organizations and community partners, including Women’s Foundation California, Oakland Interfaith Gospel Choir and Faith in Action, for a Legacy Event. The gathering explored how lifetime and planned gifts can sustain arts organizations. It also went beyond encouraging donations. Stagebridge shared a blueprint for hosting legacy events, offering other nonprofits a practical model for bringing supporters, advisors and community partners together to learn about long-term giving. Executive Director Michelle Lagunas Taylor said, “We wanted to share what we’ve learned so other organizations can build on it. The future of the arts depends on all of us finding ways to work together and support one another.” Stagebridge knows firsthand what a legacy gift can make possible. We extend our deepest gratitude to Claire Wahrhaftig, whose visionary legacy gift provided vital support for Stagebridge during our post-pandemic recovery. Extraordinary acts of planned giving alongside ongoing support from our federal and state allocations, corporate partners, foundation grants, and dedicated donors are essential to keeping the performing arts thriving in our communities. And those performing arts classes offer something that research on social prescribing is bringing into focus: the value of making the arts part of everyday life. At Stagebridge, older adults can try acting, musical theater, improvisation, clowning and singing. They can learn something new, meet people and enjoy creating together. Curious about Stagebridge or new to the performing arts? In December, Stagebridge is offering weekend workshops as a fun, low-pressure way to try your hand at stand-up comedy, introductory musical theater, and more before winter term begins in January. Learn more about classes at Stagebridge.org and ways to give at Stagebridge.org/donate. Senior artists and legacy donors help build a meaningful and vibrant creative community at Stagebridge.

pages.text: Wednesday, October 28, 2026 27 Wine Corner Continued from page 20 André and Mireille Tissot: A family estate If Dugois represents continuity, the Domaine André et Mireille Tissot tells a story of tradition meeting experimentation. Founded by André and Mireille Tissot in Montigny-lès-Arsures in 1962, the domain became one of the Jura’s most influential estates under their son Stéphane and his wife, Bénédicte. Stéphane joined the family business around 1990 and gradually transformed its approach to viticulture and winemaking. The estate’s vineyards expanded substantially, and organic and biodynamic farming became central to its philosophy. The domain’s current presentation describes approximately 35 hectares under biodynamic cultivation, while published profiles have reported larger totals at different times, reflecting changes in the estate’s holdings. Stéphane Tissot’s defining ambition has been to reveal the individuality of the Jura’s vineyards. Rather than treating Chardonnay or Savagnin as uniform products, he makes wines from particular sites, including La Mailloche, Les Bruyères and En Barberon. Differences in soil, exposure, vine age and cellar treatment become part of the final expression. His range extends from finely judged Chardonnay and Savagnin to Pinot Noir, Poulsard and Trousseau, alongside traditional regional specialties. Some whites are matured without the protective topping-up of barrels, allowing a veil of yeast to develop and contribute the region’s characteristic oxidative notes. Others are ouillés — topped up to limit oxygen exposure — and offer a fresher, more fruit-driven interpretation of the same broad grape varieties. The contrast is important. Jura whites are not all oxidative, nor does every bottle taste of walnuts and bruised apples. A carefully made, topped-up Chardonnay may be taut, citrusy and mineral, while a Savagnin matured under flor can be savory, saline and richly complex. Tissot has also explored alternative vessels, including amphorae, and different approaches to maceration and fermentation. Such experimentation is not innovation for its own sake; it is an attempt to find the most appropriate means of expressing each grape and vineyard. His wines have helped bring the Jura to a wider international audience, demonstrating that its traditions can be both preserved and reinterpreted. Under Stéphane and Bénédicte, the family domain has become a meeting point between rigorous vineyard practice, technical curiosity and an unusually broad range of styles. Overnoy-Crinquand: The living memory of rural Jura In Pupillin, a village overlooking the vineyards near Arbois, Domaine Overnoy-Crinquand offers a different perspective. Here, the story is not simply about wine, but about an older form of rural life in which vines, livestock and agricultural land remain part of a single working enterprise. Associated with the GAEC de la Bidode, the estate is run by the Crinquand family, with Mickaël Crinquand responsible for the winegrowing side. The family Cedric and Stephane Tissot at Domaine Tissot Cedric with the large collection of Vin Jaunes at Domaine Tissot Domaine Overnoy-Crinquand in the village of Pupillin continues the traditional practice of polyculture, combining winemaking with dairy farming and the cultivation of feed crops. This approach has become increasingly unusual as specialist wine estates have expanded and agricultural activities have separated. At Overnoy-Crinquand, however, the vineyard remains part of a broader farming landscape. The estate has a long-standing commitment to organic agriculture, with certification dating to 1999 according to published accounts. Its vineyards, covering roughly 5.5 hectares in commonly reported descriptions, are devoted to Chardonnay, Savagnin, Ploussard and Trousseau. The wines are made on a small scale, with an emphasis on the local character of Pupillin. Ploussard is perhaps the most evocative expression of the domain. Its color can be surprisingly light, sometimes resembling a deep rosé in the glass, but its appeal lies in its aromatic detail rather than its concentration. Red berries, woodland fruit and lively acidity can combine with a delicate, almost transparent texture. In the right hands, this is a wine of subtlety rather than power. Trousseau provides a contrasting expression, with more color, body and structure. The whites add further variety, from Chardonnay to Savagnin, while the estate also produces traditional regional styles and a distinctive specialty known as Velours du Jura. The latter does not carry the Macvin appellation because of its method of production. Overnoy-Crinquand’s appeal lies partly in this sense of continuity. Its wines are rooted in a landscape where farming remains tangible and practical, rather than being reduced to a collection of fashionable techniques. The result is an authentic expression of a village whose identity is inseparable from its vineyards. Three domains, one distinctive region What unites these three producers is not a single style of wine, but a shared respect for the individuality of the Jura. Dugois demonstrates the appeal of traditional varieties, careful cellar work and an evolving commitment to organic viticulture. Stéphane and Bénédicte Tissot show how biodynamic farming and experimentation can reveal the character of individual vineyard sites. Overnoy-Crinquand preserves a small-scale, mixed-farming tradition while producing wines that remain closely connected to the identity of Pupillin. Together, they illustrate why the Jura cannot be understood through a single bottle or grape variety. Its reds can be light or structured; its whites fresh and mineral or deeply savory; its sparkling wines lively and its Vin Jaune contemplative and longlived. Food offers another route into Mickaël Crinquand, proprietor of Domaine Overnoy-Crinquand the region’s wines. Ploussard is a natural partner for roast chicken, charcuterie, mushrooms and soft cheeses. Trousseau can stand up to duck, pork and richer meat dishes. Chardonnay works well with freshwater fish, poultry and Comté, while Savagnin and Vin Jaune are classic companions to mature Comté, morels and cream-based dishes. These are wines that reward attention without demanding ceremony. They can be enjoyed young for their freshness or cellared when their structure and style justify it. Some are immediately welcoming; others unfold slowly in the glass. The Jura’s growing reputation brings opportunities as well as challenges. Greater international demand can introduce unfamiliar drinkers to the region, but it can also make sought-after bottles harder to find and risk turning a diverse wine culture into a fashionable commodity. The three domains considered here offer a reminder of what makes the Jura worth discovering in the first place: family histories, distinctive grape varieties, varied farming practices and a willingness to let place speak through wine. but is essentially dry. articles.text: Editor: We are pleased to support Adam Hundt’s candidacy for Piedmont City Council. In getting to know Adam, we’ve been struck by his genuine commitment to civic service and his thoughtful, open-minded approach. He listens carefully and seeks to understand the concerns and priorities of Piedmont residents. Adam brings a fresh perspective grounded in his experience in business and public policy. His practical approach to making sustainability affordable, his focus on strong police and fire services, wildfire preparedness, and safer streets makes him well suited to serve our community. As a father raising young children in Piedmont, he also brings a meaningful long-term view to the decisions shaping our city’s future. Piedmont values engaged residents, and we believe Adam would honor that tradition while contributing sound judgment, new ideas, and a collaborative spirit. We enthusiastically support his election. –Jennie Stomberg & Morry Jones
articles.title: Adam Hundt for City Council

articles.text: Dear Editor: It is an honor to support Tom Ramsey’s re-election to our City Council. Tom and I met the usual Piedmont way, through our kids; Tom has lived in Piedmont for 30 years with his wife and has two daughters who attended Piedmont schools. He has volunteered on our Planning Commission for seven years, including one as Chair. He’s a practicing architect and Vice President of a national construction project management company. Over the many years we have volunteered together, leading low-income housing repair projects with Piedmont Community Service Crew students, I have become increasingly convinced of his thoughtfulness and commitment to our community. Tom is even-tempered, a good problem-solver who works well with others, understands Piedmont, and gets stuff done. He will bring an open, fact-based, and logical approach, along with an appreciation for maintaining and improving our amazing town of Piedmont. –Steve Schiller Piedmont Soccer Club President (former), PRFO Founder, Piedmont Climate Task Force Member (former), PCSC Boy Scouts Volunteer, and PUSD substitute teacher.
articles.title: Support Tom Ramsey’s re-election

articles.text: Dear Editor: I am writing to encourage my fellow Piedmonters to vote for Nancy Beninati for City Council. I had the pleasure of working with Nancy when we served on the Board of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont. I found her to be hardworking, intelligent, and someone who gets things done. Nancy’s public service to both the Piedmont community and the State of California, through her civil rights work at the Department of Justice, has given her valuable experience to serve on the City Council. Over the past few weeks, I have read the candidate questions and answers published in the Piedmont Post, and Nancy’s responses have been thoughtful, practical, and grounded in a deep understanding of the issues facing our city. She knows our community and brings the experience and skills that will serve us well. I am excited to vote for Nancy Beninati for Piedmont City Council on November 3, and I hope you will too. –Cathie Geddeis Former President, League of Women Voters of Piedmont; Former Piedmont School Board Trustee
articles.title: Vote for Nancy Beninati

articles.text: Dear Piedmont: I want to share with you why I support Tom Ramsey for re-election to City Council. I have lived in Piedmont for the past 26 years and over those years our City has faced many challenges. Tom Ramsey knows Piedmont and has worked on numerous City commissions and committees over the years. He has a deep understanding of the issues that our City faces. He listens and considers the input of residents. He is solution oriented. articles.text: in Wonderland, Desousa acted as lead parade ambassador and expert candy distributor. The procession of the parade was a bit different this year, with the brass band Orchestra Euphonos and a Fenton’s bicycle cart leading the way for Desousa and Gina Johnson-Geiger, the owner of Kollektiv Clay Studio. “We were throwing out candy just onto the street, like a giant street piñata. It was awesome. The kids were going crazy, chasing after the candy in the street,” said Desousa. Parade weather could not have been more ideal, the moderate weather allotted for any costume, including those with stuffy masks, full pajamas or crop tops. The parade drew out thousands of costumed guests to freely haunt the street looking for treats from 11:00 a.m.-1:00 p.m. “I completely ran out of candy and started giving away older decorations. We haven’t run out of pumpkins yet though,” said Jon Goldstein owner of the Pumpkin Patch attached to J. Miller Flowers. Desousa has owned Valentine’s baby & kids for almost 13 years, and just this year finally got to participate in the heart of the event, by being on the street. “I’ve been the main organizer [of the parade] for the last three years. It was actually the first year that I have been able to be on the street enjoying it, and not only that, but I was in it! I’m usually just trapped in my shop, so that was very different and really fun,” said Desousa. This year the parade did away with the truck driving in the street and the bagpiper, going with footand pedal-power and the brass band instead. The parade started down by Pet Food Express, the site of the dog costume contest. Goldstein, who has run his pumpkin patch for 30 years on Piedmont Avenue, approved of throwing the event a week early on Saturday, October 24 instead of the 31st. While the Halloween spirit in kids is abundant enough for a week-plus of celebration, parents may lament over the bountiful stashes of sugar inducing tantrums a full seven days before the big night of trick-or-treating. The parade in its 39th year provided a full day of fun for the whole family. When the street opened back up at 1:00 p.m. costumes were still the rule not the exception for the afternoon. The party continued with pumpkins at Mountain View Cemetery and a carnival at Piedmont Avenue Elementary School. “I don’t think it’s a day that any of the merchants consider a money maker, to be honest. We do it for the community, and it’s just a really fun tradition. We just do it because it’s really fun and all the families and the kids who grow up around here love it,” said Desousa.

articles.text: The final days of the Wildwood Pumpkin Patch loom near as the pumpkins keep selling like hotcakes and Giant Jack prepares for his big teleportation trick. The past weekend, October 23-25, kept dad and student patch volunteers busy, as Halloween approaches. Sales at the patch this past weekend were gourd-geous in comparison with the previous weekend, October 16-18. Net sales increased 71% weekend over weekend and the number of pumpkins sold skyrocketed to 1,756. The quality and magnitude of the pumpkins this year has contributed to an increase in popularity for the most traditional Halloween accoutrement, the orange carver. “Unlike years past, we’ve had some enormous carving pumpkins. Larger than any I’ve seen in the eight years I’ve been working the pumpkin patch, and they are absolutely gorgeous with long thick stems. They’ve become very popular!” said Patch Papa Nathan DeBode (left), Ronan Walsh, Fiadh Walsh, Chloe DeBode, and Eabha Walsh help out at the Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch. Photos by Brian Fischer and Vik Deshpande Student Pumpkin Patch volunteer Fiadh Walsh shows coloring sheets turned in for free Wee-Be-Little pumpkins. Matt Derrigo. The Wildwood Dads Club (WWDC) will announce the winner of Giant Jack today, Wednesday, October 28. One lucky family will welcome the plump pump to their abode. The Pumpkin Patch officially closes on Saturday, October 31 at 4:00 p.m., or earlier if the stock runs out. “We’ve completely sold out of pumpkins for the past three years, leaving some families empty-handed. With the pace of sales we’re seeing, we encourage everyone to come early, grab their Halloween pumpkins, and support Wildwood while they still can,” said Patch Papa Brian Fischer. WWDC’s largest volunteer event and fundraiser of the year, which directly supports Wildwood kids and teachers. Recent projects at Wildwood that were funded by WWDC include: a computer lab upgrade, a new A/V system in the auditorium and a new dishwasher in the staff lounge. Go to Wildwooddadsclub.org/ pumpkin-patch for a sneak peek of the impressive pumpkin variety on site. articles.text: “Measure GG provides an opportunity to help ensure that Piedmont continues to be the safe, beautiful and exceptionally well-served community we know and love.” — Teresa Baum, Realtor “The strength of our public schools is intertwined with the strength of our City. Piedmont voters passed Measure H to support our schools, and now it’s time for voters to pass Measure GG to support our City.” — Ruchi Medhekar, President, PUSD Board of Education “Our neighboring communities have all increased their transfer taxes far higher than Measure GG. A long-overdue increase in the transfer tax would provide the City with revenue to continue to provide essential services upon which we all rely.” — Bob McBain, Former Mayor; Chair of the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee Measure GG is a modest increase to Piedmont’s Transfer tax. The transfer tax is collected only when a home is sold. All of the funds generated by Measure GG will stay right here in Piedmont. Piedmont has not increased its transfer tax in 33 years but the cost of labor and materials to repair our crumbling streets and maintain our aging facilities has been skyrocketing. Our neighboring cities have responded with increased transfer tax rates and it’s time for Piedmont to do the same.
